content: Individuals living with HIV are at a heightened risk of rapid progression of tuberculosis (TB). As part of TB management, HIV testing and counseling should be offered to all individuals, including the biological children of adults living with HIV. If visiting the home or workplace of the index patient is not feasible, the patient can be interviewed at a healthcare facility, and their contacts can be listed using alternative communication methods such as telephone, email, or through intermediaries or treatment providers. Healthcare workers must systematically follow up with the index patient, intermediaries, and treatment providers to ensure all relevant contacts are mobilized to the healthcare facility. At the facility, these contacts should undergo symptom screening, chest X-rays (CXR) if applicable, TB testing, and evaluation for TB infection and eligibility for TB preventive treatment (TPT). Transportation vouchers may be necessary to facilitate this process if it occurs at a clinic. The primary focus of contact investigation should be on household members. However, contacts at workplaces, residential care facilities, schools, long-term care facilities, prisons, correctional facilities, and acute medical care facilities should also be considered, especially when exposure is likely to have been prolonged, and the index case is highly infectious. Indicators of high infectiousness include prolonged coughing, medium or high semi-quantitative results from rapid molecular testing, or extensive cavities visible on CXR. Maintaining confidentiality during contact investigation is challenging due to the social connections between index patients and their contacts. All individuals involved should be treated with respect, and confidentiality should be preserved as much as possible. National guidelines on data protection, confidentiality, privacy, and informed consent must be strictly adhered to. Contact screening is generally well-received by communities when they understand that it is conducted to protect vulnerable individuals and the broader community. If the index patient is hesitant to provide information about their household and social contacts, counseling efforts should continue over time to build trust. Coercion must be avoided, and the success of the contact investigation should not be linked to the patient’s TB treatment. Information gathered during interviews should be documented in the patient’s medical records. Contact investigation is also crucial among family members and close contacts of individuals who have died from TB. Standardized tools and protocols for data collection, entry, and analysis should be used to monitor the outcomes of contact investigations. This includes tracking the number of contacts identified, those who complete the investigation process, and the proportion of individuals diagnosed with TB disease or infection. Such data can inform program adjustments. Respecting privacy and human rights is paramount. Individuals with TB should not be compelled to disclose contacts or ensure the completion of contact investigations. Safeguards must be in place to protect the privacy, confidentiality, and human rights of all involved, while also minimizing stigma and discrimination. Key steps in contact investigation include reviewing available information on the index patient, assessing the duration and degree of infectiousness, counseling the index patient, enumerating household and close contacts, and developing a plan for investigation in consultation with the patient or their guardian. Home visits or invitations to health centers for TB screening and testing should be conducted, and treatment for TB disease or TPT should be provided as per eligibility. Ongoing support should be offered until treatment completion. Efforts should be made to follow up on missing contacts and complete any gaps in information. Examples of facilityand community-based approaches to TB contact investigation highlight the importance of adapting strategies to local contexts. For instance, in sub-Saharan Africa, the Elizabeth Glaser Pediatric AIDS Foundation implemented systematic household contact investigations under the CaP-TB project. This initiative targeted children and adolescents under 15 years of age who were contacts of index TB cases. Facility-based models involved asking index patients to bring their household child contacts to the facility for TB screening and TPT evaluation. Community-based models relied on community health workers (CHWs) to conduct household visits, screen for TB, and assess TPT eligibility using child-adapted tools. Key components of successful interventions include dedicated human resources, initial and refresher training for CHWs and healthcare workers, on-site coaching, reimbursement for transportation and food costs, and the use of standardized tools for recording and monitoring contact investigation activities. Community education and sensitization about the importance of contact investigation and TPT are also critical. Challenges such as financial constraints, lack of human resources, transportation barriers, and caregiver reluctance to initiate TPT for asymptomatic children must be addressed through targeted actions. These include advocacy for funding, hiring additional CHWs, providing transportation reimbursements, and developing educational materials for caregivers. Community-based models have proven effective in minimizing missed child contacts and ensuring better adherence to TPT. Programs like Vikelá Ekhaya in Eswatini demonstrate the feasibility and success of community-based TB contact management. This program used mobile teams to screen household contacts, assess TPT eligibility, and monitor adherence within participants’ homes. Such initiatives highlight the potential for locally adapted, differentiated, community-based interventions to improve TB prevention and care outcomes.
